aid-cryptographic-model.text: What ships, and the accepted design

Unless a paragraph below is marked as preprod or main today, it describes the accepted design. In that design an identity is active until it is convicted: there is no owner exit, no parking and no revival. A duplicity proof enters pending custody; its associated Registry fold makes it convicted (terminal); there is no withdraw; a deposit rotation is the unfreeze; and the poison, the owner's own lock on the checkpoint, lasts one epoch and is cleared by rotation. Play the checkpoint simulation. What ships today is the V1 checkpoint with role addresses.
A KERI AID is an Autonomic Identifier from the Key Event Receipt Infrastructure. Standard transferable AIDs use an E-code BLAKE3 digest of their inception event.
cardano-keri uses that qualified AID in two different but connected places:
The asset name is not a second identity. It is a domain-separated blake2b_256 hash of the qualified AID bytes, chosen because Blake2b is a native Plutus builtin:
The checkpoint policy ID plus this asset name identifies the sovereign checkpoint UTxO.

genesis-byte-binding.text: Plutus has no native BLAKE3 builtin, so a dedicated Aiken policy performs this work in a premint transaction and creates a deterministic fact token. Register then consumes and burns the token while the registration observer checks the event's semantic projection.
The observer requires the new datum to match the event's:
current controller keys and weighted threshold;

It also verifies controller signatures and witness receipts over the exact inception bytes. Copying a public inception cannot give a registrant different keys, because the signed event fixes those keys.

checkpoint-datum.text: The V1 checkpoint is list-shaped so a single key is only the smallest threshold case:

Thresholds may be integer or weighted KERI clauses. The datum well-formedness rules reject empty or malformed key sets, invalid weight encodings, unsatisfiable clauses, duplicate material where prohibited, and inconsistent sequence fields.

pre-rotation.text: KERI commits to successor keys before they become current. The checkpoint stores the standard KERI next-key digests:
Advance reveals the next keys and checks them against those stored commitments. It also applies KERI's dual-threshold rule:
signatures satisfy the new event's current threshold; and
the revealed keys satisfy the previous checkpoint's committed next threshold.
A thief with only the old current keys cannot pick an unrelated successor.

witness-binding.text: Controller authority and public KERI acceptance are separate.

For incoming toad > 0, Advance requires enough Ed25519 witness receipts over the exact rotation bytes from the incoming witness set. A witness-set change is validated against that incoming set, matching the event being activated.
A checkpoint with toad = 0 is explicitly witnessless. Applications that require public witness acceptance must reject it by policy.

sequence-and-event-binding.text: consumes the exact current checkpoint outref;
binds to the stored native KERI prior event;
accepts one next KERI event rather than skipping a history segment; and

Signed Cardano message fields bind the deployment, policy, AID-derived asset, exact spent outref, prior state, created state, and event evidence. A signature from one deployment or input cannot authorize another.

cbor-determinism.text: Cardano-side signed messages use canonical Plutus Data CBOR. Constructor indices, field order, integer encoding, and list order are protocol surface. The validator reconstructs each message from trusted transaction context and the small set of supplied evidence before serializing it for signature verification. It never asks a prover which bytes should be signed.

KERI events follow a different rule: proofs carry the exact native KERI event bytes. The checkpoint logic verifies those bytes and their semantic projection; it does not translate an event into a new CBOR representation and then claim that the new bytes are the KERI event.

domain-separation.text: Independent uses have independent, versioned domains:

The asset derivation also includes the 0x45 E-code byte before the raw AID. Changing a domain, constructor index, or field order requires a new protocol version. The old shared Merkle Patricia Forest domains discussed in the historical vetting record are not part of the sovereign checkpoint wire.

the-deposit-intent.text: A hunter froze Alice's checkpoint because its premium pool was short: the hunter took the freeze bond B, and the checkpoint cannot be consumed until the bond is back. Alice restores it with her next witnessed rotation, choosing the deposit bond option. Anyone may submit the rotation, so the choice of the deposit must come from Alice herself: her new current keys, the keys of the epoch the rotation opens, sign a deposit intent. Nobody else can choose the deposit for her rotation, and her signature cannot be replayed on another checkpoint, another rotation, another output or another chain.

The diagram reads in words: Alice's new keys sign the intent for the exact output being advanced and the amount the deposit moves. Whoever submits the Advance carries the rotation event and those signatures. The validator never takes the intent from the submitter: it rebuilds it from the output it spends, the network it is applied to and its own policy, serialises it, and counts the signatures of the rotation's current keys over those bytes. When they meet the rotation's threshold, the successor is unfrozen and holds the bond again.

The model states the intent in CardanoKeri.CheckpointDeposit: the record DepositIntent, its Plutus Data serialisation DepositIntent.preimage, the intent the validator requires intentFor, and the concrete reading of "the keys of the epoch the rotation opens signed the deposit" (Evidence.authorizes, ReadsDeposit). The intent is Plutus Data constructor 0 with eight fields, in this order: the domain tag, the network, the checkpoint policy, the spent output reference, the AID, the new sequence number, the new epoch and the amount. The table gives each value and the replay it stops.

Each signature is an Ed25519 signature over the serialised intent, carried as a position in the rotation event's current keys and the signature bytes. A position outside the keys never counts, a repeated position counts once, and a signature that does not verify never counts. The counted positions must satisfy the rotation event's current threshold.
What the model proves about these bytes (in CardanoKeri.CheckpointDepositGoals):
two intents with the same bytes are the same intent, so changing any field changes the bytes (preimage_injective, intentFor_preimage_eq_iff);
the amount the intent names is the amount the deposit step brings in, the freeze bond when frozen and nothing when not (intentFor_deposit, deposit_step_moves_named_amount);

under the concrete reading, every deposit step carries the new keys' signature over exactly the intent for its spent output and amount, and a deposit is enabled whenever that signature and the witnessed rotation are there, on a frozen or an unfrozen checkpoint (deposit_step_requires_signed_intent, deposit_enabled, unfrozen_deposit_accepted_for_zero);

signatures made over one intent authorize no other, and signatures that verify under none of the rotation's current keys never count (authorization_does_not_transfer, signed_for_one_not_another, only_new_keys_count).
The Advance is refused when the intent is missing, signed below the new threshold, signed by the old keys, or names another AID, rotation, epoch, output, policy, network or amount.

Four decisions shape the intent. It names the exact output being advanced, not only the identity and the rotation, so a freeze that races Alice's signature makes her sign again for the frozen output. It names the amount that moves, not the constant bond. A deposit on an unfrozen checkpoint is accepted with an intent naming zero, not refused. And the bytes are fixed in the model, with vectors, before any validator is written. The table names the rejected alternatives.

The checked vectors are lean/checkpoint-deposit-vectors.json, written by lean/CheckpointDepositDriver.lean: for each spent state and observed network, policy, output and AID, the intent and its bytes; candidate intents accepted or refused for a state, one row per changed field; and signature sets with whether the deposit rotation is taken. Their signatures are symbolic, a named test key over a named row's bytes; an implementation reproduces each row with real Ed25519 signatures by its own test keys. scripts/check-consumer-design.sh regenerates the vectors, refuses any difference from the committed file, and requires every changed field of every committed row to fail.

What this does not establish: Ed25519 verification is a cryptographic primitive the model takes as a parameter; that one signature cannot verify over two different messages is an assumption stated where it is used; the threshold is read as the model's KERI threshold over key positions, and the correspondence of the datum's threshold encoding and its evaluation with that reading is not claimed here; reading the network, the policy and the spent output from the transaction is the validator's obligation. No validator implements the deposit option yet.

duplicate-registration-residual.text: There is no global AID registry or mint-once absence proof. Two independent transactions may create candidates with the same policy and asset name.
This is handled by an explicit consumer rule:

A third-party registrant cannot take over the AID, because the public inception fixes the controller keys. They can only fund another candidate controlled by the same event, creating ambiguity and donating the escrow.

role-and-identity.text: The datum does not carry a caller-selectable lifecycle status. ACTIVE, ARMED, and FROZEN are distinguished by script role addresses around the same AID-derived token. Conviction has no role address: it burns the token, so a consumer meets an absent checkpoint rather than a terminal status.
The token identifies the checkpoint lineage. The role determines whether a consumer may use it. Only ACTIVE is acceptable.

v1-boundaries.text: The current V1 story covers independent, nondelegated AIDs. It does not yet cover:

non-establishment events: interaction (ixn) events are not projected, so anything they anchor — credential issuance and revocation in particular — is invisible to the checkpoint (see Compromise of the current keys);
a production-size inception beyond the current single-proof boundary;
automatic discovery of unseen KERI events.

The real three-of-seven registration story #139 adds a multi-transaction BLAKE3 proof for its 1083-byte-class inception. Delegation and recovery require a versioned proof protocol, not unchecked fields added to V1.
